Where it began

Tagenarine Chanderpaul was born in Georgetown, Guyana, on 31 May 1996, the eldest son of the West Indies batter Shivnarine Chanderpaul. With a father like that, a bat was never far from reach, and he piled up runs for Guyana's youth sides. He was the West Indies board's Under-19 cricketer of the year in 2013, and that same season Guyana gave him his first-class debut at 16, against the Leeward Islands in North Sound.

He went to the 2014 Under-19 World Cup in the UAE, and a few seasons later he got to share a dressing room with his father. In 2017, against Jamaica, the two of them both made fifties for Guyana in the same match, something no father and son had managed in first-class cricket for many years.

The player

He was a left-handed opener who liked to bat for a long time. His maiden first-class hundred, against Barbados in 2018, took him 275 balls, and a year later his 117 against the Windward Islands took 484. In 2021-22 he was the second-highest run-scorer in the regional four-day competition, averaging 73.16.

That earned him a West Indies A call and then the 2022 tour of Australia. He made his Test debut in Perth that November, receiving his cap from Brian Lara, and made a fifty in his first innings. Three months later, against Zimbabwe, he turned his first Test hundred into 207 not out and was named player of the match. By November 2026 he had played 15 Tests, making 758 runs at 28.07.

What made him special

Concentration runs in the family. In that Zimbabwe Test he and his captain, Kraigg Brathwaite, put on 336 for the first wicket, the first opening stand of 300 or more for the West Indies, beating a record that had stood for 33 years.

The big scores did not always come as often in Tests as they did in Guyana, and an opener's life against Australia's new ball can be a short one. On a good day, though, he could make bowlers wonder if he would ever get out.

Away from the middle

He has a film credit, too. In the Bollywood film 83 he played the West Indies batter Larry Gomes. Facing a film camera, he may have found, was a good deal more relaxing than facing the new ball.

And finally

When he made his first-class debut, his father was away playing in the Bangladesh Premier League and missed it. Shivnarine made up for it a few years later in the best way possible, by walking out to bat alongside him.
